edges.label: The marker signals that the first number is being revised.
The corrected number replaces the earlier one.

lessons.summary: Organise a short Spanish message around audience, purpose and required content, then revise language and coherence.
objectives: Match a message to its audience.
explanation: A short message needs an identifiable purpose and the information its reader needs. An informal invitation can greet a friend, propose an activity, give a time and ask for a reply. A formal enquiry uses a more formal greeting and consistent usted forms where direct address is needed. The same memorised paragraph will not fit every task; use the prompt to choose content and register.

Plan before writing, then revise in separate passes. First check whether all requested points are answered and whether the sequence makes sense. Next check verb forms, noun-adjective agreement, accents and opening question marks. Model texts are examples rather than compulsory scripts. A different greeting or closing may be suitable in another Spanish-speaking context, provided the relationship and purpose remain coherent. These tasks use fictional recipients, so no real personal information or message sending is required.
keyIdeas: Purpose determines content.
Register should remain consistent.
Content review and language review serve different checks.

definitions.meaning: The intended recipient or reader.
A greeting opening a message.
A closing expression suited to the relationship and message.

method: Identify audience, purpose and required points.
Plan the order of information.
Draft linked sentences in a consistent register.
Review task coverage, grammar and punctuation.

workedExample.prompt: Original task: write an informal invitation to fictional friend Ana to visit the park tomorrow at four and ask for a reply.
steps: Greeting and plan: Hola, Ana: ¿Quieres ir al parque mañana?
Time: Podemos quedar a las cuatro.
Reply request and closing: ¿Puedes confirmarlo? Un abrazo, Leo.
workedExample.conclusion: The invitation gives activity, day, time and a reply request. Other natural informal wording is valid.

misconceptions.mistake: Using a memorised text that misses a required point.
misconceptions.correction: Check the prompt against the finished message.

misconceptions.mistake: Switching between informal and formal address without a reason.
misconceptions.correction: Choose forms suited to the intended relationship.

practice.prompt: Order these parts of a fictional invitation: closing; greeting; activity and time; request for a reply.
solution: Greeting; activity and time; request for a reply; closing.
Another order can work if the message remains natural and complete, but this is a clear default.

practice.prompt: Correct the original sentence “Hola Ana quieres venir manana?” with appropriate Spanish greeting and question punctuation and correct manana to mañana using ñ.
hints: Use a greeting boundary, opening question mark and mañana.
solution: Hola, Ana: ¿Quieres venir mañana?
Hola, Ana. ¿Quieres venir mañana? is also valid.

practice.prompt: Write a short formal Spanish enquiry to a fictional museum asking its opening time and whether booking is necessary. Include a suitable greeting and closing.
hints: Use two clear questions; the museum name is unnecessary.
solution: Possible response: Estimado equipo del museo: ¿A qué hora abre el museo? ¿Es necesario reservar? Muchas gracias por su ayuda. Atentamente, Alex.
Other consistent formal greetings and closings are valid.

practice.prompt: Write a short Spanish message asking friend Sara to bring a notebook tomorrow.
solution: Hola, Sara:
¿Puedes traer un cuaderno mañana, por favor?
Gracias. Nos vemos mañana.
successCriteria: ¿Puedes traer un cuaderno mañana, por favor?

practice.prompt: An invitation says “Ven a la reunión mañana” but gives no place or time. Add fictional details and explain the improvement.
solution: Ven a la reunión mañana a las cinco en la biblioteca.
A las cinco supplies the time.
En la biblioteca supplies the place, so the reader can act on the invitation.
successCriteria: Ven a la reunión mañana a las cinco en la biblioteca.
A las cinco supplies the time.
En la biblioteca supplies the place, so the reader can act on the invitation.

notes.title: Writing structures in context
paragraphs: A short written message needs a clear purpose, the required practical details and a suitable relationship with the reader. An informal invitation can greet a friend, propose an activity, give time and place, and request a reply. Use paragraphs or short connected sentences to group information. Check that pronouns and verb forms remain consistent with tú or usted. A correct but incomplete message may fail to communicate the task: an invitation without a location leaves the reader unable to act. Revise content before adding decorative expressions.

workedExamples.prompt: Original task: invite friend Diego to a school exhibition on Saturday at eleven, meeting at the entrance.
steps: Open and propose: Hola, Diego: ¿Quieres venir a la exposición del colegio el sábado a las once?
Add the meeting point and reply request: Podemos encontrarnos en la entrada. ¿Te viene bien?
workedExamples.conclusion: The message supplies activity, day, time, location and a clear invitation to respond.

flashcards.front: What practical details does an invitation need?
flashcards.back: Activity, time and place, plus any relevant arrangement.

flashcards.front: How can a friend be asked to reply?
flashcards.back: ¿Te viene bien? or Escríbeme para confirmar.

flashcards.front: Why check tú/usted consistency?
flashcards.back: Mixed forms can make the relationship and address unclear.

flashcards.front: What should be revised before style?
flashcards.back: Missing task details and unclear meaning.

diagrams.title: Writing structures: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Purpose → Details → Response. A reply request allows the arrangement to be confirmed.

nodes.label: Response
nodes.detail: Ask whether the arrangement suits him.

edges.label: The purpose determines which details are necessary.
A reply request allows the arrangement to be confirmed.

lessons.summary: Interpret selected Spanish expressions in context and choose natural equivalents instead of literal word-for-word translations.
objectives: Choose wording suited to context and register.
explanation: An idiomatic expression can have a meaning that cannot be recovered by translating each word separately. Echar una mano commonly means to help someone, not to throw a hand. In a classroom request, ¿Me echas una mano? can mean Can you give me a hand? The English expression is also non-literal. A neutral paraphrase such as ¿Puedes ayudarme? can preserve the practical meaning.

Estar en las nubes can describe someone who is distracted or daydreaming. Do not confuse it with estar por las nubes, which can describe a very high price. Context decides whether a phrase is literal or figurative and whether it suits the relationship. These selected expressions are not a requirement to fill every answer with idioms. Accurate ordinary language is preferable when an expression’s meaning or register is uncertain; valid regional alternatives should be explained in context.
keyIdeas: Translate the intended meaning.
Small preposition changes can change an expression.
Use idioms only when context supports them.

definitions.meaning: A conventional multiword expression functioning as a unit.
To help someone in the uses practised here.
To be distracted or daydreaming in the figurative use practised here.

method: Read the complete context.
Check whether a literal meaning fits.
Identify the conventional meaning and register.
Choose a natural paraphrase or equivalent.

workedExample.prompt: Original fictional classroom exchange: “No entiendo este ejercicio. ¿Me echas una mano?” Explain the request in English.
steps: The speaker says they do not understand the exercise.
Echar una mano asks for help in this context.
A natural translation is I do not understand this exercise. Can you give me a hand?
workedExample.conclusion: The request is for assistance, not a physical hand. Can you help me? also preserves the meaning.

misconceptions.mistake: Translating every word literally.
misconceptions.correction: Use context and the expression’s conventional meaning.

misconceptions.mistake: Confusing en las nubes with por las nubes.
misconceptions.correction: Check the preposition and what the expression describes.

practice.prompt: Paraphrase “¿Me echas una mano?” in neutral Spanish.
solution: ¿Puedes ayudarme?
¿Me ayudas? is also suitable in many informal contexts.

practice.prompt: Original fictional context: “Pablo no oyó la pregunta; estaba en las nubes.” Explain the idiom in English without diagnosing a health condition.
hints: Use the figurative meaning supported by the sentence.
solution: He was distracted or daydreaming. The sentence also says he did not hear the question.
The sentence does not establish a medical condition.

practice.prompt: Explain the difference between these original sentences: “Ana está en las nubes” and “Los precios están por las nubes.”
hints: Compare both the subject and the preposition.
solution: Ana is distracted or daydreaming in the figurative reading.
The prices are very high.
En and por are part of different expressions here; translating both the same way loses meaning.

practice.prompt: Translate “I agree with you, but I want to think a little more.”
solution: Estoy de acuerdo contigo.
Pero quiero pensar un poco más.
Combined: Estoy de acuerdo contigo, pero quiero pensar un poco más.
successCriteria: Pero quiero pensar un poco más.
Combined: Estoy de acuerdo contigo, pero quiero pensar un poco más.

practice.prompt: Explain “Me di cuenta de que faltaba una página” in English and identify what was realised.
hints: Treat darse cuenta as one expression.
Find the clause after de que.
solution: The sentence means “I realised that a page was missing.”
Me di cuenta expresses the act of realising.
The missing page is the information that became apparent.
successCriteria: The sentence means “I realised that a page was missing.”
Me di cuenta expresses the act of realising.
The missing page is the information that became apparent.

notes.title: Idiomatic language in context
paragraphs: An idiomatic expression has a conventional meaning that may not follow directly from its individual words. Learn it in a situation and with the surrounding grammar. Tener ganas de means to feel like doing something and takes an infinitive when followed by an action. Estar de acuerdo expresses agreement, while darse cuenta de means to realise. Avoid inserting idioms merely to sound advanced; an unsuitable expression can obscure a simple message. When explaining an idiom, give its communicative meaning and a context in which it is natural.

workedExamples.prompt: Original exchange: “¿Vamos al parque?” “Hoy no tengo ganas de salir.” Explain the response.
steps: Tener ganas de salir means feeling like going out, not possessing something called ganas.
No negates the desire in the current situation.
workedExamples.conclusion: The speaker says they do not feel like going out today; the line does not necessarily reject the friend or all future outings.

flashcards.front: Translate “I feel like reading”.
flashcards.back: Tengo ganas de leer.

flashcards.front: What does estar de acuerdo mean?
flashcards.back: To agree.

flashcards.front: What does darse cuenta de mean?
flashcards.back: To realise or become aware of something.

flashcards.front: Why learn an idiom in context?
flashcards.back: Its meaning, register and grammar may not follow from a literal word-by-word translation.

nodes.label: Meaning
nodes.detail: I do not feel like going out.

nodes.label: Scope
nodes.detail: Today’s preference, not a permanent refusal.

lessons.summary: Plan and review a Spanish practice task using its actual instructions rather than an invented universal exam formula.
objectives: Identify task requirements and allowed resources.
explanation: Start with the actual task: identify audience, purpose, required points, response language and any word or time limit. Follow the rules supplied by your teacher or assessment provider about dictionaries, notes and repeated listening. MYP year alone does not determine a learner’s language phase or the format of every school assessment. The timing examples here are hypothetical practice plans, not official exam requirements.

Allocate time for planning, drafting and checking in proportion to the task. In review, first check whether you answered the question and preserved any source information. Then check tense, agreement, accents and punctuation. A few accurate connectors can clarify a response; forced complexity can obscure it. Rehearsing a strategy is useful, but completing a practice task does not prove a CEFR level or guarantee a mark. Model responses illustrate criteria rather than replace your teacher’s assessment guidance.
keyIdeas: Read the actual task rules.
Review content before surface detail.
A practice plan is not an official exam format.

definitions.meaning: The instruction specifying what a task requires.
Preparation of content and structure before drafting.
Checking and improving a response against the task and language requirements.

method: Extract required content, audience and constraints.
Set a feasible practice plan.
Draft a response focused on the task.
Check coverage, meaning, grammar and punctuation.

workedExample.prompt: Hypothetical 40-minute writing practice: allocate 5 minutes to planning, 28 to drafting and 7 to reviewing. Check the total and explain the review order.
steps: The allocations total 5 + 28 + 7 = 40 minutes.
First check required points, audience and meaning.
Then check verbs, agreement, accents and punctuation.
workedExample.conclusion: The plan fits this practice period. Adjust it to the actual task; it is not an official timing rule.

misconceptions.mistake: Assuming every exam uses the same timing or word limit.
misconceptions.correction: Read the specific instructions.

misconceptions.mistake: Polishing grammar while leaving a required point unanswered.
misconceptions.correction: Check content coverage first.

practice.prompt: Original fictional task: “Write an informal email inviting a friend to a club. Include the day, time and one reason to join.” List the required content and register.
solution: Informal email to a friend.
An invitation including the day, time and one reason to join.

practice.prompt: Task: write an informal email inviting a friend to a club, including the day, time and one reason to join. A fictional response says “Hola, Ana: Ven al club el jueves. Es divertido. Un abrazo, Leo.” Identify the missing required detail and supply a suitable Spanish addition.
solution: The time is missing.
Possible addition: La reunión empieza a las cinco.
Other consistent meeting times are valid.

practice.prompt: For a hypothetical 30-minute writing practice, propose planning, drafting and checking times that total 30 minutes, and name two checks.
hints: Use a plan, not an asserted official rule.
solution: Possible plan: 4 minutes planning, 21 drafting and 5 checking; total 30 minutes.
Check every required content point, then check verb forms and agreement.
Other workable allocations totalling 30 minutes are valid.

practice.prompt: A hypothetical 25-minute writing practice reserves 4 minutes to plan and 6 to review. How long remains to draft, and why preserve review time?
solution: 25 − 4 − 6 = 15 minutes remain for drafting.
Review can identify missing required information.
It can also correct verb agreement and tense errors that change meaning.
successCriteria: Review can identify missing required information.
It can also correct verb agreement and tense errors that change meaning.

practice.prompt: A task asks for two reasons, but a draft gives one reason in three different sentences. Explain the problem and a repair.
solution: Repeating one reason does not fulfil the request for two.
Keep the clearest version of the existing reason.
Add a genuinely different reason, for example convenient timing as well as interest in the activity, if both fit the fictional scenario.
successCriteria: Repeating one reason does not fulfil the request for two.
Keep the clearest version of the existing reason.
Add a genuinely different reason, for example convenient timing as well as interest in the activity, if both fit the fictional scenario.

checklist: I plan within the time available.

notes.title: Exam strategies in context
paragraphs: Assessment practice should begin with the actual task instructions, not an assumed universal format. Identify the required audience, purpose, word guidance and content points before drafting. In language work, a concise response that communicates all requested information is more useful than a long response with invented detail and confused verbs. Review in layers: task completion, verb agreement and tense, then spelling and accents. A rehearsal checklist supports self-review but is not an official marking scheme or a guarantee of a grade.

workedExamples.prompt: Original practice task: write an informal message with a plan, time and reason. A draft says “Voy al club porque es interesante.” Identify what is missing and repair it.
steps: The draft states a plan and a reason but omits the required time.
A fuller version is: Hola, Sara: Mañana voy a ir al club a las cuatro porque hacemos experimentos sencillos.
workedExamples.conclusion: The revision addresses practical information and audience before seeking more elaborate vocabulary.

flashcards.front: What should be checked first?
flashcards.back: Whether the response fulfils the actual task and required content points.

flashcards.front: Why review verbs before decorative vocabulary?
flashcards.back: Incorrect person or tense can change who acts and when.

flashcards.front: What does a practice checklist establish?
flashcards.back: A structure for self-review, not an official score.

flashcards.front: How can planning prevent omission?
flashcards.back: List each required detail and match it to a planned sentence.
